title: Chapter 2.  History — Ancient & Medieval Tribal Kingdoms

blocks.content: Meghalaya's pre-colonial history centres on three parallel indigenous political traditions - the Khasi Hima confederacy system, the Jaintia kingdom, and the Garo clan-based social structure - each organised quite differently from the large centralised monarchies more familiar from mainland Indian history.

Rather than a single unified Khasi kingdom, the Khasi Hills were traditionally organised into a number of small, independent, self-governing chiefdoms/states called 'Hima', each headed by a hereditary or elected chief (Syiem), with the Hima of Khyrim and Hima of Mylliem (both centred near present-day Shillong) among the more historically prominent of these numerous small polities.

This decentralised, federated Hima system - rather than a single monarchy - is a distinctive feature of traditional Khasi political organisation, and elements of it (traditional chieftainships, village councils called 'Dorbar') continue to operate today alongside the modern constitutional/administrative structures covered in Chapter 5, reflecting a notable degree of institutional continuity.

★ EXAM POINT: The Khasi Hills were NEVER unified under a single traditional kingdom - instead, they comprised numerous small, independent 'Hima' chiefdoms (such as Khyrim and Mylliem), each led by a Syiem - a frequently tested distinguishing fact from the more centralised Jaintia kingdom below.

Unlike the decentralised Khasi Hima system, the Jaintia Hills were historically united under a single, more centralised Jaintia kingdom, ruled by the Jaintia Raja from a capital that shifted at different points in history (including Jaintiapur, now in present-day Bangladesh, reflecting the kingdom's historically wider territorial extent before later boundary changes).

The Jaintia kingdom had significant historical and cultural interaction with neighbouring Bengal and Assam, and - notably - its rulers adopted elements of Hindu religious practice at various points (a degree of Sanskritic/Hindu influence less pronounced in traditional Khasi Hima political culture), even while much of the wider Jaintia populace retained indigenous belief systems.

The Garo Hills traditionally lacked centralised kingdoms altogether, organised instead around a clan-based ('Chra'/'Machong') social structure with village-level ('Nokma'-headed) authority - the Nokma being a customary landholding/village-head institution, closely linked to the Garo's distinctively matrilineal inheritance system (Chapter 8).

This absence of centralised Garo political authority meant the Garo Hills historically experienced a comparatively later and more gradual, piecemeal process of external political integration (first by neighbouring regional powers, then British colonial administration) compared to the more institutionally structured Khasi Hima and Jaintia kingdom systems.

items: Khasi Hills: traditionally organised into numerous small, independent 'Hima' chiefdoms (e.g. Khyrim, Mylliem), each led by a Syiem - never a single unified kingdom.
Jaintia Hills: united under a single, more centralised Jaintia kingdom, historically capitaled at Jaintiapur (now in Bangladesh); rulers showed some Hindu religious influence.
Garo Hills: no centralised kingdom; clan-based ('Chra'/'Machong') social structure, village authority vested in the 'Nokma', linked to Garo matrilineal inheritance.
